name: Formal Methods for Security
description: Formal verification, proofs, and verified implementations of security-critical systems and protocols.

ccs.narrative:
Formal methods for security at CCS has expanded from protocol verification toward hardware, smart contracts, and compiler correctness. A Formal Analysis of 5G Authentication (CCS 2018) set the tone for the dataset period: using Tamarin and ProVerif to find gaps in the 5G AKA protocol before widespread deployment. 5GReasoner: A Property-Directed Security and Privacy Analysis Framework for 5G Cellular Network Protocol (CCS 2019) extended this to cross-layer properties, discovering new attacks the standard had missed.

Smart contract verification arrived with eThor: Practical and Provably Sound Static Analysis of Ethereum Smart Contracts (CCS 2020), which provided a sound abstract interpreter for EVM bytecode. Machine learning safety was formalized in Quantitative Verification of Neural Networks and Its Security Applications (CCS 2019), linking verification with robustness certificates. InSpectre: Breaking and Fixing Microarchitectural Vulnerabilities by Formal Analysis (CCS 2020) brought formal analysis to bear on CPU-level leakage.

Secure compilation against microarchitectural adversaries was formalized in Exorcising Spectres with Secure Compilers (CCS 2021), which defined the threat model and proved that specific compilation strategies are sound. EasyPQC: Verifying Post-Quantum Cryptography (CCS 2021) extended the EasyCrypt proof assistant to cover post-quantum scheme security proofs, keeping formal verification pace with the post-quantum migration.

ndss.narrative:
Formal methods for security at NDSS have concentrated on bringing machine-checked rigor to protocols that real users depend on. ZEUS (NDSS 2018) and LTEInspector (NDSS 2018) represent the field's early high-water marks: the former verified smart-contract safety via abstract interpretation and model checking, the latter systematically tested 4G LTE protocols with adversarial model-based techniques, uncovering a range of practical attacks on cellular infrastructure.

The 2019–2021 period showed formal methods migrating to newer targets. Component-Based Formal Analysis of 5G-AKA (NDSS 2019) decomposed the next-generation cellular authentication protocol into verifiable components; A Systematic Framework to Generate Invariants for Anomaly Detection in Industrial Control Systems (NDSS 2019) bridged formal invariant synthesis and ICS anomaly detection; and PHOENIX (NDSS 2021) brought runtime monitoring of cellular protocol state to devices in the field.

Recent contributions have targeted emerging protocol surfaces. Extrapolating Formal Analysis to Uncover Attacks in Bluetooth Passkey Entry Pairing (NDSS 2023) extended formal prover scope to include human-machine interaction steps; A Unified Symbolic Analysis of WireGuard (NDSS 2024) gave the modern VPN protocol a comprehensive symbolic treatment; and PropertyGPT (NDSS 2025) experimented with LLM-driven property generation to bootstrap formal verification of smart contracts. Together these efforts chart a path from hand-crafted models toward semi-automated formal security assurance.

sp.narrative:
Formal methods at IEEE S&P span protocol verification, smart-contract analysis, speculative execution modeling, and machine-checked cryptographic proofs. The 2018 cohort tackled two distinct targets: AI2: Safety and Robustness Certification of Neural Networks with Abstract Interpretation (S&P 2018) applied abstract interpretation to ML robustness, while DEEPSEC: Deciding Equivalence Properties in Security Protocols Theory and Practice (S&P 2018) advanced automated verification of observational equivalence for cryptographic protocols.

The 2019-2020 wave brought verified implementations and smart-contract verification. Simple High-Level Code for Cryptographic Arithmetic (S&P 2019) and EverCrypt: A Fast, Verified, Cross-Platform Cryptographic Provider (S&P 2020) demonstrated machine-verified cryptographic code at production performance. VerX: Safety Verification of Smart Contracts (S&P 2020) applied reachability analysis to Ethereum contracts, and VERISMART: A Highly Precise Safety Verifier for Ethereum Smart Contracts (S&P 2020) improved precision. Spectector: Principled Detection of Speculative Information Flows (S&P 2020) formalized Spectre leakage as a semantic property amenable to static analysis.

Hardware-Software Contracts for Secure Speculation (S&P 2021) established a formal contract between ISA and microarchitecture for speculative security, while The Provable Security of Ed25519: Theory and Practice (S&P 2021) closed a longstanding gap between the informal security argument and formal proof for a widely-deployed signature scheme.

By 2022-2024, formal methods permeated multiple S&P tracks—appearing in blockchain, TEE, and applied-crypto papers—reflecting the community's growing expectation that security claims should be accompanied by machine-checkable proofs rather than informal arguments.

uss.narrative:
The earliest listed work shows formal methods being pointed at two very different targets at once. On the systems side, "HeapHopper: Bringing Bounded Model Checking to Heap Implementation Security" (USENIX 2018) used bounded model checking to find exploitable heap-metadata bugs in real allocators, while on the protocol side "Modelling and Analysis of a Hierarchy of Distance Bounding Attacks" (USENIX 2018) extended the applied pi-calculus to reason about distance-bounding security symbolically. The same year, "Formal Security Analysis of Neural Networks using Symbolic Intervals" (USENIX 2018) pushed formal reasoning into a brand-new domain, certifying robustness properties of deep neural networks. So from the start the area split along three threads: verifying implementations, analyzing protocols, and certifying learned models.

The next shift, around 2019-2021, was toward fully verified implementations rather than just bug-finding. "VRASED: A Verified Hardware/Software Co-Design for Remote Attestation" (USENIX 2019) and "EverParse: Verified Secure Zero-Copy Parsers for Authenticated Message Formats" (USENIX 2019) delivered machine-checked code with end-to-end security proofs, and "IODINE: Verifying Constant-Time Execution of Hardware" (USENIX 2019) brought the same rigor to leakage-free hardware. This matured into verified low-level infrastructure: "Formally Verified Memory Protection for a Commodity Multiprocessor Hypervisor" (USENIX 2021) and "DICE*: A Formally Verified Implementation of DICE Measured Boot" (USENIX 2021) proved security of the trusted-computing base itself, while "ETHBMC: A Bounded Model Checker for Smart Contracts" (USENIX 2020) carried model checking into the blockchain world.

A parallel and increasingly automated protocol-analysis line ran alongside it. "A Spectral Analysis of Noise" (USENIX 2020) gave comprehensive automated proofs over an entire family of Diffie-Hellman key-exchange protocols, "A Tale of Two Headers" (USENIX 2020) formalized inconsistent web-framing defenses, and "SmartVerif" (USENIX 2020) pushed protocol-verification automation with dynamic proof strategies. This momentum carried into wireless and cellular standards, with "Formal Analysis and Patching of BLE-SC Pairing" (USENIX 2023) and "Sherlock on Specs: Building LTE Conformance Tests through Automated Reasoning" (USENIX 2023) turning specifications themselves into objects of formal scrutiny.

Today the field is broad, applied, and tightly coupled to deployed systems. It has reached post-quantum cryptography with "Formal verification of the PQXDH Post-Quantum key agreement protocol" (USENIX 2024), blended fuzzing with formal guidance in "HyPFuzz: Formal-Assisted Processor Fuzzing" (USENIX 2023), and moved from finding flaws to automatically repairing them in "TAPFixer: Automatic Detection and Repair of Home Automation Vulnerabilities based on Negated-property Reasoning" (USENIX 2024). Alongside continued work on cellular and Bluetooth specifications like "CellularLint" (USENIX 2024) and "Finding Traceability Attacks in the Bluetooth Low Energy Specification" (USENIX 2024), the area now spans verified clouds, hardware leakage models, neural-network certification, and natural-language specs, all sharing the common goal of replacing testing intuition with proof.

top4.narrative:
The earliest papers in this list show formal methods spreading across two very different fronts at once. On the protocol side, "A Formal Analysis of 5G Authentication" (CCS 2018) and "LTEInspector" (NDSS 2018) used symbolic model checkers to find real flaws in the cellular standards that billions of people rely on, while "DEEPSEC" (S&P 2018) pushed the theory of automatically deciding equivalence properties for cryptographic protocols. On a parallel track, researchers began applying verification to machine learning and low-level systems: "AI2" (S&P 2018) and "Formal Security Analysis of Neural Networks using Symbolic Intervals" (USENIX 2018) brought abstract interpretation and interval analysis to certify neural-network robustness, and "ZEUS" (NDSS 2018) opened the smart-contract verification wave by analyzing safety of Ethereum contracts.

Two big shifts define 2019-2020. First, smart contracts became a dominant subarea, moving from bug-finding toward sound, provable guarantees: "VerX" (S&P 2020) proved functional properties, "VERISMART" (S&P 2020) targeted arithmetic safety, and "eThor" (CCS 2020) delivered a provably sound static analysis grounded in formal EVM semantics, complemented by executable Solidity semantics (S&P 2020) and bounded model checkers like "ETHBMC" (USENIX 2020). Second, verification graduated from models to real, deployed code. "Simple High-Level Code for Cryptographic Arithmetic" (S&P 2019), "EverCrypt" (S&P 2020), and "The Last Mile" (S&P 2020) produced machine-checked, high-speed cryptographic implementations all the way down to assembly, while "EverParse" (USENIX 2019) and "VRASED" (USENIX 2019) verified parsers and a hardware/software remote-attestation co-design. The 5G/cellular thread also matured with "5GReasoner" (CCS 2019) and component-based 5G-AKA analysis (NDSS 2019).

The Spectre disclosures triggered a third wave: formalizing microarchitectural leakage. "Spectector" (S&P 2020) gave a principled semantics for detecting speculative information flows, "InSpectre" (CCS 2020) formally modeled and fixed microarchitectural vulnerabilities, and "Hardware-Software Contracts for Secure Speculation" (S&P 2021) introduced a contract abstraction that was consolidated by "SoK: Practical Foundations for Software Spectre Defenses" (S&P 2022). Information-flow guarantees also reached hardware in "HyperFlow" (CCS 2018) and whole systems in "A Secure and Formally Verified Linux KVM Hypervisor" (S&P 2021).

By 2021-2023 the field reads as a maturing discipline: systematization papers like "SoK: Computer-Aided Cryptography" (S&P 2021) survey the toolchain, foundational protocols get end-to-end treatment ("The Provable Security of Ed25519", S&P 2021; "The EMV Standard: Break, Fix, Verify", S&P 2021), and core tools themselves are re-engineered, as in the major "ProVerif with Lemmas, Induction, Fast Subsumption" overhaul (S&P 2022). The frontier now reaches richer properties and shared infrastructure: temporal properties of contracts ("SmartPulse", S&P 2021), compiler infrastructure spanning proof systems and verification ("CirC", S&P 2022), distributed-systems foundations ("Foundations of Dynamic BFT", S&P 2022), and economic/game-theoretic security ("Clockwork Finance", S&P 2023) — extending formal reasoning from "is this code correct" to "is this system's incentive structure safe."
